claims.text: During cooling, high-temperature disordered BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially undergoes spinodal decomposition.
Spinodal decomposition produces Ni–Al-lean BCC1 and Ni–Al-rich BCC2 regions.
Below the ordering temperature, the Ni–Al-rich regions order into B2 precipitates.
Annealing temperature modulates the extent of spinodal decomposition and subsequent ordering.
Higher annealing temperatures promote a larger BCC fraction.
Higher annealing temperatures promote more pronounced Ni–Al partitioning.
Ni–Al partitioning and ordering produce a hierarchical microstructure and increased hardness.
The hierarchical microstructure consists of a Ni–Al-lean BCC matrix containing Ni–Al-rich ordered B2 nanoparticles and larger B2 particles.
Larger B2 particles can themselves contain Ni–Al-lean BCC nanoparticles.
The microstructure contains minor FCC precipitates, including grain-boundary Widmanstätten side-plates.
On cooling from the disordered BCC state, the alloy enters a miscibility gap.
The phase boundaries and compositional modulation created by segregation and ordering hinder dislocation motion.
Hindrance of dislocation motion increases hardness.
A larger volume of high-temperature BCC at higher annealing temperatures enhances decomposition and ordering kinetics.
The 1100 °C annealed and quenched baseline has a near-equal BCC/FCC mixture.
The 1100 °C baseline has minimal ordering features and the lowest hardness in the temperature series.
Relative to 1100 °C, annealing at 1200 °C and 1300 °C will produce a higher BCC fraction and clearer Ni–Al partitioning.
Relative to 1100 °C, annealing at 1200 °C and 1300 °C will produce a higher density and more pronounced ordering of Ni–Al-rich B2 precipitates.
Relative to 1100 °C, annealing at 1200 °C and 1300 °C will increase Rockwell C hardness.
Slower cooling or conditions outside 1100–1300 °C may alter or obscure the sequential spinodal-decomposition and ordering pathway.
